name: Azhagiyanathar Temple, Tiruvamathur
deity: Shiva as Azhagiyanathar (Abhirameswarar), with the goddess Muthambikai
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Nadu Nadu country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century) by all three of its saints; structural temple of Chola, Vijayanagara and later patrons
dynasty: Medieval Tamil patrons (Chola, Vijayanagara and later)
summary: Azhagiyanathar, the beautiful Lord, worshipped also as Abhirameswarar, is the Shiva temple of Tiruvamathur near Villupuram, a Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Nadu Nadu country and one of the rare shrines sung by all three of the great Tevaram saints, Sambandar, Appar, and Sundarar.

sections.history: Tiruvamathur stands a few kilometres north-west of Villupuram in the old Nadu Nadu country, the region of the Tamil land whose Shiva temples were sung by the saints of the Tevaram. The temple of Azhagiyanathar is one of these Paadal Petra Sthalams, and among them it holds a rare distinction: it is counted among the few shrines praised in song by all three of the great hymnists, Tirugnana Sambandar, Appar, and Sundarar. Tradition holds that Sundarar came here on his southward journey toward Tiruvarur. The Lord is worshipped as a swayambhu linga, a form said to have risen of itself, and is honoured both as Azhagiyanathar, the beautiful one, and as Abhirameswarar. The shrine is an old foundation, traced by tradition to the Pallava and Chola ages, renewed by later inscriptional patrons and enlarged in the time of the Vijayanagara kings, and it has been kept in worship down the long centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple is a spacious Dravidian complex that in fact holds two temples within one enclosure. The sanctum of Azhagiyanathar enshrines the swayambhu linga of the Lord, while the goddess Muthambikai is given not merely a shrine but a full temple of her own, with its own gopuram and its own surrounding shrines for the attendant deities, an arrangement that marks her special honour here. Inscriptions in the temple record renovation by a Tamil sovereign of the Kopparakesari title, and the principal structure is credited to the Vijayanagara ruler Achyuta Deva Raya, so that the building as it stands carries the work of several ages. The precise sequence and dates of its construction are not fully settled in the sources.
sections.legends: The name Abhirameswarar is tied by tradition to the worship of Rama. It is told that Rama himself came to this place and worshipped the Lord, and that from his adoration the deity took the name Abhirameswarar, the Lord who was pleasing to Rama, and the altogether lovely one. The same beauty of the deity is carried in the Tamil name Azhagiyanathar, the beautiful Lord. That the three saints of the Tevaram all sang here is itself remembered as a sign of the sanctity of the shrine, and Sundarar's visit on his journey south is kept in the temple's lore.
sections.festivals: As at every Shiva temple, Maha Shivaratri is observed as the great night of the year, and the monthly Pradosham twilight is kept with devotion. The festival months of the Tamil calendar bring the temple's processions and the worship of the sixty-three Nayanmar saints, and the goddess Muthambikai, honoured in her own temple, receives her own observances. Being a village temple, its calendar follows the Tamil almanac and local custom, so devotees are advised to confirm the festival days and car festival timings with the temple before visiting.
sections.experience: Tiruvamathur lies close enough to Villupuram to be reached easily, yet keeps the quiet of a country shrine. The pilgrim can honour the swayambhu Lord Azhagiyanathar in his sanctum and then cross to the separate temple of the goddess Muthambikai, a rare chance to worship the Mother in a shrine raised wholly to her, complete with its own tower. Devotees dwell on the memory that Sambandar, Appar, and Sundarar all stood here and sang, and that Rama is said to have worshipped at this very place; to walk the enclosure is to follow where the saints walked. The temple rewards an unhurried visit, within sight of the fields of the Nadu Nadu country.

visit.timings: Generally open in the morning from about 7:30 am until noon, and again in the evening from about 5 pm until 8:30 pm; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruvamathur lies about 7 km north-west of Villupuram, along the Villupuram–Tiruvannamalai road. Villupuram, the district centre, is the nearest major railway junction and bus hub, with Chennai and Puducherry within reach by road. Buses on the Tiruvannamalai road pass near the village, and local transport from Villupuram brings the visitor to the temple.
